text: Hi everyone! Welcome to LS2: Free Time, Live! In this short video, you'll see your goals, your final product, and the grammar and words you need.
Our big question is: what do we really do in our free time? We look at hobbies and events, like a match, a concert or a Saturday at the skate park.
You have four goals. One: understand short vlogs, posts and web pages about hobbies. What are people doing now, and what do they usually do?
Two: check if a web page is reliable. Who wrote it? When? Why? Then make a fact file and give credit to your sources.
Three: speak live, like a vlogger. Say what people are doing now, and compare it with what they usually do.
And four: write a vlog script, with tips for a healthy use of screens.
At the end, you make your own Free Time Vlog: a video of one and a half to two minutes about a hobby or an event, with Google Slides and your face in a small window.
It has seven slides: hello, what is happening now, what usually happens, a photo or facts, your likes, your screen tips, and the credits.

You work step by step: choose a hobby or event, check your source, write your script, make your slides, record, improve one part, and submit it on Classroom. A vlog buddy helps you, but every vlog is your own.
The final product is twenty-five percent of your LS mark. Your vlog counts most. Then your script and slides, your source, your fact file, and your work on every step.
Now, the grammar. The star of this LS is the Present Continuous: am, is or are, plus a verb ending in i-n-g. I'm watching a match. They're playing volleyball. Are you having fun? Yes, I am!
Careful with the spelling: dance, dancing. Swim, swimming. Play, playing.

Compare it with the Present Simple: the Present Simple for what you usually do, the Present Continuous for now. I usually play football on Saturdays, but today I'm watching a match. And some verbs, like like and know, never take i-n-g. Say: I like it.
For likes, use love, like, don't like or hate, plus i-n-g: I love skating. And for screen tips, use imperatives: Take a break. Don't use your phone in bed.

And the words you need: free-time activities, like go swimming or do karate. Clothes and kit, like trainers or a helmet. The weather. Events, like a match or a festival. Time words, like now and at the moment. And screen words, like screen time.
Do the learning paths in order. Each one gives you a piece of your vlog, so at the end your vlog is easy to make. Have fun, and let's go live!
Hi everyone! Welcome to LS2: Seasons and Celebrations. In this short video, you'll see your goals, your final product, and the grammar and vocabulary you'll need.
Our big question is: why do we celebrate, and what can celebrations tell us about people, places and the natural world? From the Castanyada and Halloween to Thanksgiving, Diwali or Lunar New Year.
You have five goals. One: understand articles, videos and people explaining how they celebrate, and work out new words from context.
Two: check information in at least two sources, decide if they're reliable, and credit them.
Three: explain a celebration to people who don't know it: its customs, its dates, its origins, and what it means to the people who celebrate it.
Four: compare it with a local celebration, find links between cultures, and avoid stereotypes.
And five: plan a school celebration day, and propose it to the head teacher in a formal email.

Your final product is a Celebration Day Proposal. In groups of three or four, you design a respectful celebration day at school around one tradition. Your group records a two to three minute video pitch with Google Slides, and everyone speaks. Then, each of you writes a formal email to the head teacher.

You work in steps: choose a celebration, research it, plan the day, make the slides, rehearse and record the pitch, and write the email. At every step, you hand in your own short task, so your teacher can see your work.
The final product is twenty-five percent of your LS mark, and your mark is your own. Your part of the pitch counts most, then your email, your source, teamwork, and your work on every step.

Now, the grammar. To describe customs, use the Present Simple: People decorate their houses. Children dress up. And useful chunks: It is celebrated on the thirty-first of October. It takes place in November. Careful with on, in and at!

To explain origins, use the Past Simple and used to: It started in sixteen twenty-one. People used to light bonfires. And to add information, use relative clauses: a festival which marks the harvest, people who travel home.

To plan the day, you need the future. Going to for plans: We're going to decorate the hall. Will for decisions and predictions: I'll bring the music. Everyone will love it. The Present Continuous for arrangements: We're meeting the head teacher on Monday. And the Present Simple for timetables: The event starts at ten.

For the email, be polite and formal: Dear Ms Smith, I am writing to propose a celebration day. Could we use the school hall? I look forward to hearing from you. And to compare cultures: both, similar to, different from, and whereas.

And the vocabulary: seasons and weather, like chilly, or the days get shorter. Celebrations, like a parade, fireworks and decorations. Verbs, like dress up, light candles and get together. Feelings, like grateful and proud. And planning, like set up and send invitations.
Do the learning paths in order: each one gives you a piece of your final product. So, which celebration will you bring to school? Let's celebrate!
